column4: The source's root ك ذ ب describes falsehood that shows in conduct; this ayah opens the opposite path with a person who gives and is mindful of God, making generosity an enacted confirmation.
The next ayah says this giver confirms the best; it supplies the truthful inward stance that the source contrasts with a life that only looks right.
This ayah says God will ease such a person toward ease, completing the sustained giving path that the source's interrupted-run idiom lacks.
The passage turns to the one who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; this is the practical opposite of giving and encouragement to give in the section.
This ayah says the miser denies the good; the source's root ك ذ ب likewise connects denial to a visible life, and here denial is joined directly to withholding.
The next ayah says God will ease that person toward hardship, completing the consequence of the withholding-and-denial path.

The deeds of disbelievers are likened to a mirage that looks like water but yields nothing when reached; this is a precise Qur'anic surface that promises substance but has none, like the source's painted cloth.
The next likeness is layered sea darkness in which even a hand is hard to see; it supplies the converse of the cloth's deceptive visibility, showing the hidden reality after 24:39's false appearance.

These people walk when lightning gives light and stop when darkness returns; that exact start-and-halt movement parallels the source's animal that runs one stretch then stops and its prayer abandoned when no one watches.
The preceding parable says a fire briefly lights the surroundings and then God takes away its light; that exposed, temporary appearance introduces the intermittence completed by 2:20.

This ayah sets the second parable in a storm with darkness, thunder and lightning; the next ayah's walking-then-stopping is its own added detail and the specific link to the source's interrupted motion.
This parable opens with owners of a garden who intend to harvest it; the following verses reveal their plan to withhold its crop from the poor, continuing the section's provision scene.
The garden owners make no exception in their plan; this detail frames the refusal to share that becomes explicit in 68:24.
They urge one another to go harvest their crop; this starts the purposeful movement whose hidden aim is revealed in the next verses as keeping the poor out.
This ayah asks whether people think they can merely say “we believe” and be left untested; it raises the difference between a surface claim and a life whose truth is shown in the next ayah.
The next ayah says God tests people to distinguish the truthful from the liars; the source's root ك ذ ب similarly treats truth or falsehood as something manifested beyond a spoken claim.
Some people twist their tongues with scripture so listeners think their words come from the Book, though they do not; this is a specific verbal surface that imitates a real underlying pattern.

This ayah describes people who write a text with their own hands and claim it is from God for a price; the counterfeit object and its false claim directly echo the source's fabricated-looking cloth and lie-in-action root.

The ayah says some conceal what God revealed and sell it for a small price; it adds the specific deed of hiding truth behind an outward transaction, which the source's inner-intention image makes perceptible.

This ayah recalls a covenant to make scripture clear rather than conceal it, then says they cast it aside and sold it cheaply; it gives a concrete broken obligation next to the praise-for-unearned-credit detail in 3:188.
People make scripture into sheets, displaying some and concealing much; this specific selective covering resembles the source's surface pattern that gives an incomplete account of what lies beneath.
On the Day of Judgment mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to deeds; the body's own state exposes action, like the source's cloth that says nothing yet tells a lie by its condition.
This ayah says tongues, hands and feet will testify to what people did; it repeats the specific image of bodily action disclosing what a person might wish to conceal.
Hearing, sight and skin testify against people about what they did; this directly parallels the source's claim that a person's state can tell the truth of their actions without a verbal confession.
The next ayah says the people ask their own skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak; it completes the bodily-witness image begun in 41:20.
This ayah says they had not hidden themselves from their own hearing, sight or skins; it makes the gap between concealment and actual exposure explicit after the testimony in 41:20–21.
People emerge separately to be shown their deeds; this is a direct judgment scene for the source's claim that a life's acts expose the truth of its outward religious claim.
The next ayah says whoever did an atom's weight of good will see it; it specifies that even a small real act is exposed.
This ayah applies the same measure to an atom's weight of evil; it completes the source's image of deeds, rather than appearances, being answerable.
The ayah says guardians are appointed over people; it supplies the watching context for the source's idea that hidden intent and visible actions answer to judgment.
The next ayah describes those recorders as noble scribes; it specifies the record behind the judgment introduced in 82:10.
This ayah says the recorders know what people do; it directly joins inner accountability to the actual conduct that the section uses to expose denial.

The source's dictionary idiom describes an attack whose start may fail to continue; this ayah begins a sequence of steeds charging at speed, whose following actions carry the motion through rather than stopping.
The next ayah has the steeds strike sparks as they run; this is the continuing force of the charge begun in 100:1.
This ayah moves from the charge to a dawn raid, another step in the sustained attack opposite to a charge that peters out.
The steeds raise dust in their charge; this ayah contributes the continuing physical effect of motion before its completion in 100:5.
The sequence ends with the steeds breaking into the midst of a group; this completes the attack that the source's negative idiom says may halt before its intended blow.
This ayah calls the disbelievers' worship at the Sacred House whistling and clapping; it is a specific outward religious performance whose substance does not match the name, unlike real prayer.

The source's root س ه و distinguishes being away from prayer from being inattentive to a part within it; this ayah uses the same root for people immersed in confusion, a related heedlessness outside the prayer setting.

After condemning words unsupported by deeds in 61:2–3, this ayah praises people who stand together like a solid structure; the real, joined structure contrasts with the source's cloth that only looks woven.

The ayah commands the Prophet not to drive away people who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face; it directly reverses pushing the vulnerable away and makes intention, rather than public adornment, the measure.

This repeated command says not to repel those who call on God morning and evening, seeking His face; it gives another specific reversal of the orphan-pushing image and contrasts devotion with audience-facing display.
Trade does not distract these men from God's remembrance, prayer and almsgiving; the ayah supplies sustained worship and giving as a direct opposite to prayer abandoned when unobserved.

This ayah forbids those with bounty to swear that they will stop giving to relatives, needy people and migrants; it directly addresses a beginning-to-stop gift and commands its continuation and forgiveness.

This ayah says those who unjustly consume orphan property are consuming fire; it gives a specific harmful act toward the orphan that confirms the section's claim that the denial is exposed in conduct.

This ayah pairs careful treatment of an orphan's property with full, just measure; it is a concrete boundary against the section's displaced care and the shortfall that makes an outward exchange false.
Shu'ayb's people are told to give full measure and weight and not deprive others; that explicit fair-exchange boundary reverses the source's root ك ذ ب as a lie enacted in behavior.
This ayah commands full measure and weight and forbids depriving people of their due; it is another direct boundary for dishonest outward dealing.
The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance sets a specific standard for an exchange whose appearance must match what is actually delivered.
The people are told to give full measure and not be among those who defraud; this is a direct reversal of a life that lies through its actions.
The next ayah says to weigh with a straight balance; it supplies the concrete measure standard following 26:181.
This ayah forbids depriving people of their due or spreading corruption; it completes the fair-measure warning with the actual harm that a false exchange causes.
This ayah commands maintaining the balance with justice and forbids shortfall; its exact boundary against withholding a due amount fits the source's action-level falsehood.
